Re: 
CMS-0062-P – Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs  
91 Fed. Reg. 19890 (April 14, 2026) 
Dear Secretary Kennedy and Dr. Oz:  
The American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network (ACS CAN) appreciates the opportunity to comment 
on the policy changes to the 2026 Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs proposed 
rule. ACS CAN is making cancer a top priority for public officials and candidates at the federal, state, and 
local levels. ACS CAN empowers advocates across the country to make their voices heard and influence 
evidence-based public policy change, as well as legislative and regulatory solutions that will reduce the 
cancer burden. As the American Cancer Society’s (ACS) nonprofit, nonpartisan advocacy affiliate, ACS 
CAN is more determined than ever to end cancer as we know it, for everyone. 
We applaud the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) for proposing to extend the requirements 
established in the 2024 Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization final rule for the Prior 
Authorization Application Programming Interface (API) to prescription drugs. Including prescription drugs 
would simplify the prior authorization process for providers and reduce confusion and lead to more timely 
access for patients. We support many of the proposals outlined in the proposed rule and support CMS’s 
efforts to improve alignment of standards across payers. We note that the proposed rule does not extend 
these new requirements to Part D plans, and we encourage CMS to address this in future rulemaking.  
ACS CAN offers comments on the following policies: 
• 
Interoperability Standards for Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) 
• 
Electronic Prior Authorization for Drugs 
• 
Improving Communications and Decision Timeframes for Prior Authorizations 
• 
Requirements for Issuers That Offer Small Group Market Qualified Health Plans on the Federally-
facilitated Small Business Health Options Program Exchanges 
• 
Updates to Patient Access, Provider Directory, Provider Access, and Payer-to-Payer APIs; API 
Usage Metrics 
• 
Requests for Information: Step Therapy 
• 
Requests for Information: Laboratory Tests and Durable Medical Equipment, Prosthetics, 
Orthotics, and Supplies Items 
 
II. PROVISIONS OF THE PROPOSED RULE  
A. Interoperability Standards for Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) 
American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network 
HHS Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs Proposed Rule 
June 15, 2026 
Page 2 
 
 
CMS outlines the importance of additional implementation guides (IGs) for certain interoperability APIs. 
Although CMS is not proposing to require or recommend the CARIN Consumer Real-Time Pharmacy 
Benefit Check (RTPBC) IG, CMS seeks comment on whether it should do so and whether providing patients 
with real-time prescription cost and coverage information through the Patient Access API would be 
valuable. 
ACS CAN supports providing patients with clear, timely access to their own benefit and coverage 
information through the Patient Access API. Cancer patients often require tailored treatment regimens, 
which may involve multiple, concurrent prescription drugs. Because coverage rules, prior authorization 
requirements, and out-of-pocket costs can vary widely across patients and medications, navigating these 
benefits can be confusing and burdensome. It is crucial for patients to have access to their real-time drug 
costs and coverage to help them understand what they owe and make informed decisions about their 
treatment. 
B. Electronic Prior Authorization for Drugs 
3.  
Proposed requirement to incorporate drugs covered under a medical benefit into the Prior 
Authorization API for all impacted payers  
CMS proposes to require impacted payers1 to expand the scope of the required Prior Authorization API 
adopted in 2024 to incorporate drugs covered under a medical benefit. CMS is proposing an October 1, 
2027, compliance date. CMS seeks comment on whether there are drugs other than those payable under 
Medicare Part B that should be covered by proposed prior authorization requirements for Medicare 
Advantage (MA) organizations. 
ACS CAN strongly supports including drugs in the requirements for the Prior Authorization API. We 
appreciate that CMS was responsive to our comments on the 2024 Interoperability Standards and Prior 
Authorization proposed rule. When drugs are excluded from these API requirements, providers and 
patients must navigate different timelines and requirements depending on the drug type and payer. This 
inconsistency creates unnecessary burden and can lead to treatment delays.  
Expanding the rule to cover drugs will meaningfully benefit patients who can often face unnecessarily long 
delays in obtaining their medically necessary drugs while prior authorization determinations are pending. 
Prescription drugs – whether outpatient or physician‐administered therapies – play a vital role in cancer 
care. The proposed change would simplify the prior authorization process, reduce confusion, and lead to 
more timely access. ACS CAN also supports the proposed compliance timeline given that impacted 
payers already have until 2027 to comply with requirements for non-drugs and services. 
However, the proposed rule excludes Qualified Health Plan (QHP) issuers on State-based Exchanges 
(SBEs), State-based Exchanges on the Federal Platform (SBE-FPs), and Part D sponsors from the list of 
impacted payers. We urge CMS to extend these requirements to issuers on SBEs and SBE-FPs and Part D 
sponsors to ensure consistency across programs to reduce burden on both providers and patients.  
In response to the request for comment, ACS CAN urges CMS to ensure that any drug covered by an MA 
plan is subject to the same prior authorization requirements. Applying the same standards to all drugs 
helps providers and payers follow a single process and reduces administrative obstacles that slow patient 
access to needed treatment. This consistency also gives patients clearer expectations when navigating 
 
1 “Impacted payers” in this proposed rule refers to Medicare Advantage (MA) organizations, state Medicaid and 
Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) fee-for-service (FFS) programs, Medicaid managed care plans, CHIP 
managed care entities, and Qualified Health Plan (QHP) issuers on the Federally-facilitated Exchanges (FFEs) unless 
otherwise noted. 
American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network 
HHS Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs Proposed Rule 
June 15, 2026 
Page 3 
 
 
complex care. 
4-6.  
Proposed requirement to support the National Council for Prescription Drug Programs 
(NCPDP) SCRIPT Standards 
CMS proposes to require impacted payers to meet standards for processing prior authorization requests 
for drugs covered under the pharmacy benefit by January 1, 2028. CMS also proposes that issuers meet 
standards to provide formulary and benefits information and make available real-time coverage 
information for drugs covered under the pharmacy benefit by October 1, 2027. 
ACS CAN supports this proposal. Simplifying the prior authorization process to include all prescription 
drugs will ensure one set of unified requirements across health care services, reducing confusion and 
administrative burden. This proposal also aligns with existing Part D requirements by updating the 
underlying interoperability standards that Part D plans rely on, promoting greater consistency across 
payers.  
C. Improving Communications and Decision Timeframes for Prior Authorizations 
2. 
Proposed requirement to include a specific reason for denial in response to prior 
authorization requests for all drugs 
CMS proposes requirements to further standardize the processes for providers to request and receive prior 
authorization for drugs. Beginning October 1, 2027, CMS proposes that impacted payers that deny a prior 
authorization request for any drug must provide a specific reason for the denial. This requirement already 
applies to non-drug items and services.  
ACS CAN supports requiring payers to provide a clear, specific reason for all drug-related prior 
authorization request denials. MA organizations and Part D sponsors are already subject to this 
requirement, so extending it to all impacted payers promotes consistent standards across programs. We 
previously urged CMS to include drugs in this provision in the 2024 rulemaking and appreciate CMS’s 
efforts to ensure alignment in this proposed rule.  
We agree that prior authorization denials are often insufficiently detailed, creating additional 
administrative burden for providers and prolonging the time patients wait to receive their medically 
necessary drugs. ACS CAN also urges CMS to require payers to provide more than a generic statement 
such as “failed to establish medical necessity” so providers can quickly understand and address the 
issue. 
3. 
Prior authorization decision timeframes  
Alignment across programs: CMS proposes to align prior authorization decision processes across different 
CMS programs. Under this proposal, state Medicaid fee-for-service (FFS) programs, Medicaid managed 
care plans, and CHIP managed care entities would be required to respond to expedited prior authorization 
requests for covered outpatient drugs within 24 hours and dispense at least a 72-hour supply in 
emergencies. CMS would also require state FFS programs to follow the same timeframes used for CHIP 
FFS non-drug items and services and would modify state CHIP FFS programs’ prior authorization and 
notification timeframes to align state with Medicaid FFS. CMS proposes compliance dates beginning 
October 1, 2027, for all proposals. CMS requests comment on whether future rulemaking should require 
MA organizations to respond to all prior authorization requests for drugs within 24 hours. 
ACS CAN supports CMS’s efforts to create standardized timeframes for prior authorization responses. We 
agree with shortening and aligning the state CHIP FFS drug prior authorization notification timeframe with 
state Medicaid FFS, as state-level prior authorization timeframes can vary considerably. While we support 
American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network 
HHS Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs Proposed Rule 
June 15, 2026 
Page 4 
 
 
aligning the prior authorization timeframes for these payers with those established under MA and Part D, 
we encourage CMS to ensure that those regulations reference the same underlying standards so that 
updates remain consistent across programs. In response to the request for comment, ACS CAN supports 
future rulemaking that would require MA organizations to meet the 24-hour-requirement for covered 
outpatient drug prior authorization requests – the same prior authorization requirement as used in 
Medicaid and CHIP. 
We also support the proposed 72-hour standard and 24-hour expedited prior authorization decision 
timeframes for drugs; however, we are concerned that the 7-calendar day standard and 72-hour expedited 
prior authorization decision timeframes for non-drug services finalized in the 2024 rule do not align. 
Imposing a standardized process will limit the burden on providers and patients. As such, we urge CMS to 
shorten the timeframes for non-drug services in future rulemaking to align with those proposed for drugs, 
supporting consistent standards that facilitate patient access to needed care.   
Notably, CMS does not propose any recourse for providers and patients when the payer fails to meet these 
required timeframes. ACS CAN strongly urges CMS to implement penalties for payers who fail to adhere to 
the prior authorization timeframes. CMS should monitor payer compliance and take administrative action 
when necessary to ensure patients receive timely access to treatment. 
QHP issuers on the Federally-facilitated Exchanges (FFEs): CMS proposes that QHP issuers on the 
Federally-facilitated Exchanges (FFEs) align their prior authorization decision timeframe for non-drug items 
and services with the timeframe required for non-drug items and services for other impacted providers 
beginning October. 1, 2027. CMS also proposes to extend requirements for notifying patients and providers 
of prior authorization decisions to drugs. CMS requests comment on whether QHP issuers should be 
required to notify the requesting provider of a determination in a shorter timeframe than the timeframe 
required to notify enrollees; whether the requirement to make decisions as “expeditiously as the enrollee’s 
health condition requires” is appropriate; and whether certain non-covered outpatient drugs should follow 
the 24-hour statutory requirement for covered outpatient drugs. 
ACS CAN supports efforts to standardize prior authorization requirements across payers. We believe this 
approach will reduce patient confusion and alleviate the burden on providers by simplifying prior 
authorization requirements and removing unnecessary complexity from the health care system. However, 
these provisions do not apply to QHP issuers on SBEs or SBE-FPs. We urge CMS to reconsider and 
establish standardized timeframes for all payers to respond to prior authorization requests, ensuring 
patients receive consistent protection regardless of where they live.  
Additionally, we believe the 7-calendar day standard and 72-hour expedited prior authorization decision 
timeframes for non-drug services is inadequate and does not align with the 72-hour standard and 24-hour 
expedited prior authorization decision timeframes for drugs outlined in this proposed rule. We encourage 
CMS to shorten the timeframes for non-drug services for QHP issuers on FFEs, on SBEs, and on SBE-FPs 
and all impacted payers.  
ACS CAN supports aligning the notification timeframes for QHP issuers on the FFEs so that both enrollees 
and providers receive drug-related prior authorization determinations simultaneously. If CMS shortens the 
provider notification timeframe, the enrollee notification timeframe should be shortened accordingly. Fast 
notification provides patients with more time to file an appeal if necessary or work with their provider to 
adjust their treatment plan. Delays in access to medically appropriate treatment can lead to disease 
progression, making timely decisions and notifications essential.  
We support the requirement that QHP issuers on the FFEs make decisions as the enrollee’s health 
condition requires; but only if CMS enforces the minimum timeframe that issuers must meet. Without a 
American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network 
HHS Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs Proposed Rule 
June 15, 2026 
Page 5 
 
 
minimum standard, patients may not receive consistent protection across plans. For non-covered 
outpatient drugs, if a plan is permitted to impose prior authorization, CMS should ensure consistent 
standards across all products and that they meet the same requirement as for covered outpatient drugs.  
6-7. 
Proposed requirements to publicly report prior authorization metrics for non-drug items and 
services and drugs for impacted payers 
CMS proposes new public reporting requirements for prior authorization metrics. Under this proposal, 
impacted payers would be required to report numeric counts in addition to percentages for certain existing 
metrics, publicly report additional metrics for non-drug items and services, and publish drug-related 
metrics on their public websites. Reporting would begin in 2028 using 2027 data. CMS also proposes that 
MA organizations would report at the contract level, state Medicaid and CHIP FFS programs at the state 
level, Medicaid managed care plans and CHIP managed care entities at the plan and program level, and 
QHP issuers on the FFEs at the issuer level. 
ACS CAN supports the public reporting of prior authorization metrics for both non-drug items and services 
and prescription drugs. We believe this information should appear not only on the payer websites but also 
on CMS’s website, organized by payer, to improve transparency and accessibility of the data on payer 
performance.  
Regarding reporting levels, ACS CAN believes that all payers should be required to report data at the plan 
level and not at the issuer level. Consumers enroll in individual health plans, and responsiveness can vary 
even within the same issuer. Plan-level reporting information would also allow CMS to more accurately 
determine which plans are complying with prior authorization requirements. 
We also urge CMS to require payers to report prior authorization metrics by category of item or service, 
rather than aggregating across all non-drug items and services. Aggregated data obscures whether the 
payer is imposing prior authorization requirements inappropriately for given services. Requiring payers to 
report based on category of service – such as hospitalizations, laboratory services, or imaging – would 
provide a more accurate reflection of how prior authorization is being used and could reveal, for example, 
whether a payer has an unusually high overturn rates for imaging services compared to hospitalizations. 
We also encourage CMS to use this data to conduct oversight to determine how often prior authorization 
edits are imposed and overturned, and why. It is crucial to understand how trends in prior authorization 
can be attributed to plan decisions versus outdated communication to consumers in plan documents. 
D. Requirements for Issuers That Offer Small Group Market Qualified Health Plans on the Federally-
facilitated Small Business Health Options Program Exchanges 
3. 
Patient Access API 
CMS proposes to require issuers offering small group market QHPs on the Federally-facilitated Small 
Business Health Options Program Exchanges (FF-SHOPs) to implement and maintain a Patient Access API 
conformant with certain Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources® (FHIR) standards. This requirement 
would apply to data for plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2028, with reporting deadlines beginning 
in 2029. 
ACS CAN supports this proposal because it would allow more consumers to access their own health 
information and promote greater consistency in patient access to data across markets. Additionally, QHP 
issuers on FFEs have been required to implement a Patient Access API since the 2020 final rule. Since 
many QHP issuers participate in both the FF-SHOPs and FFEs, the additional burden of extending these 
requirements to FF-SHOPs would be minimal.  
American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network 
HHS Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs Proposed Rule 
June 15, 2026 
Page 6 
 
 
5. 
Payer-to-Payer API 
CMS proposes to require issuers that offer small group market QHPs on the FF-SHOPs to implement and 
maintain a Payer-to-Payer API to support the exchange of patient health information when an enrollee 
changes payers or has concurrent coverage with multiple payers. This requirement would apply to plan 
years beginning on or after January 1, 2028.  
ACS CAN supports extending existing Payer-to-Payer API policies to small group market QHP issuers on 
the FF-SHOPs. Many cancer patients have complex care needs that require coordinated care across 
multiple specialists and subspecialists. Ensuring that patient data follows them when they change payers 
is essential to avoiding unnecessary delays in care, which can lead to worse outcomes. We also support 
requiring payers to provide plain-language educational resources about the API to enrollees and to clearly 
explain that patients may choose to opt out of the data exchange.  
F. Updates to Patient Access, Provider Directory, Provider Access, and Payer-to-Payer APIs; API 
Usage Metrics 
1. 
Information about prior authorizations for drugs in the Patient Access, Provider Access, and 
Payer-to-Payer APIs 
CMS proposes to require impacted payers to include information about prior authorization requests and 
decisions for all drugs in the data made available through their Access APIs, using the same timeframes 
established for non-drug items and services under the 2024 final rule. 
ACS CAN supports extending prior authorization data requirements to prescription drugs. Using the same 
timeframes for drugs and non-drug items and services promotes consistency across requirements and 
reduces confusion among providers, payers, and patients. We also ask CMS to clarify how individuals can 
designate caregivers access to information through the Patient Access API, and to ensure that payers must 
provide enrollees with the ability to access this information through written communication if they prefer. 
3. 
Removing drug formulary information from the Provider Access and Payer-to-Payer APIs 
CMS proposes to remove drug formulary information from the required data that must be made available 
through the Provider Access and Payer-to-Payer APIs for MA organizations, state Medicaid and CHIP FFS 
programs, Medicaid managed care plans, and CHIP managed care entities. CMS also seeks comment on 
whether there are cases in which continued access to drug formulary data through these APIs would still 
be helpful. 
ACS CAN urges CMS to reconsider this policy. Even if providers can obtain formulary information through 
other channels, having this information consolidated in one place is essential. Without it, providers would 
be forced to spend unnecessary time searching multiple sources to determine coverage, increasing 
administrative burden and potentially resulting in delays in access for patients. These APIs are intended to 
streamline and facilitate the exchange of information to support patient care and removing formulary data 
requirements undermines that purpose.  
 
 
 
American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network 
HHS Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs Proposed Rule 
June 15, 2026 
Page 7 
 
 
III. REQUESTS FOR INFORMATION 
D. Request for Information: Step Therapy 
CMS seeks comment on ways to streamline the step therapy process through technology and data 
sharing – such as the Payer-to-Payer API – to give payers access to historical patient information. CMS also 
seeks comment on how technology could support step therapy determinations and improve current step 
therapy processes, including evaluating and applying step therapy use criteria and honoring step therapy 
use criteria established by other payers. 
ACS CAN supports efforts to use technology to make step therapy more efficient; however, we urge CMS to 
exercise caution. We are concerned that the use of AI in utilization management (including prior 
authorization), coverage determinations, and claims management could result in higher rates of care 
denial and greater burden for physicians and patients, impeding timely access to evidence-based care.2 
Any technological tools, including AI applications, should be reviewed by CMS staff with appropriate 
human oversight to ensure proper safeguards for protecting patient access to medically necessary care.  
We also urge CMS to conduct rigorous oversight of plans’ use of utilization management tools, like step 
therapy, and we support providing CMS with additional resources to practice more meaningful oversight 
and enforcement. CMS should use this oversight for outpatient and physician-administered prescription 
drugs. Step therapy can be burdensome and create unnecessary delays in treatment. For cancer 
patients — whose treatment is often tailored to their specific condition — any barrier to receiving the 
specific drug they need can jeopardize treatment outcomes. Given these risks, we encourage CMS to 
require health plans to establish an override process through which providers can request an exemption 
from step therapy protocol, thereby reducing treatment delays.  
Additionally, we urge CMS to closely review how health plans are using utilization management edits to 
ensure they are being accurately recorded. In 2024, ACS CAN released a report examining 
utilization management tools for cyclin-dependent kinase 4 and 6 (CDK 4/6) inhibitors, a class of drugs 
used to treat breast cancer.3 Across the four drugs in this class (Ibrance, Kisqali, Kisqali Femara co-pack, 
and Verzenio), Part D plans required prior authorization 97 percent of the time. Although no plans 
explicitly listed step therapy in their formulary design, the report found that some plans effectively 
implemented “embedded” step therapy through prior authorization requirements – occurring in 23 percent 
of cases for Ibrance, 22 percent for Kisqali and the Kisqali Femara co-pack, and 88 percent for Verzenio. 
These onerous utilization management practices, including step therapy, impede access to 
clinically appropriate treatment and can force patients to incur additional costs to obtain the therapy best 
suited for their care. For patients with cancer, timely access to the right medication is essential to avoid 
preventable disease progression.  
E. Request for Information: Laboratory Tests and Durable Medical Equipment, Prosthetics, Orthotics, 
and Supplies Items 
CMS seeks public comment on how prior authorization for laboratory tests and durable medical 
equipment, prosthetics, orthotics, and supplies (DMEPOS) impact patient care and provider burden, and 
on potential opportunities to mitigate that burden. 
ACS CAN appreciates CMS’s recognition that prior authorization can create barriers in timely access to

care for patients. Laboratory tests are essential for cancer diagnosis, treatment selection, and patient 
monitoring, and DMEPOS items support patients in mobility, daily functioning, and symptom management. 
We recommend that prior authorization for laboratory tests and DMEPOS items be held to the same 
standards applied to other services and that CMS continue to closely monitor how payers implement these 
requirements. We also encourage CMS to exercise its oversight authority when prior authorization 
requirements for these items result in delayed treatment approvals, adding unnecessary burden for both 
patients and providers.  
 
CONCLUSION 
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the 2026 Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization 
for Drugs proposed rule. If you have any questions, please feel free to contact me or have your staff 
contact Allie Babyak, Public Policy Fellow, Access to Care and Prescription Drugs at 
Allie.Babyak@cancer.org. 
 
Sincerely, 
 
Anna Schwamlein Howard

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network (ACS CAN); signed by Anna Schwamlein Howard, Vice President, Public Policy Advocacy
- **Stakeholder type:** Advocacy Group
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** ACS CAN is the nonprofit, nonpartisan advocacy affiliate of the American Cancer Society and advocates for evidence-based policies to reduce the cancer burden.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

ACS CAN broadly supports CMS's proposal to extend 2024 interoperability and prior authorization requirements to prescription drugs, emphasizing that cancer patients need timely access to outpatient and physician-administered therapies. The organization recommends broader applicability to Part D and state-based exchange QHPs, stronger denial specificity, shorter and aligned PA timeframes, penalties for missed timeframes, plan-level and category-level metric reporting, continued formulary data access, caregiver access clarification, and strong oversight of step therapy, AI, laboratory testing, and DMEPOS prior authorization.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; API-USAGE-METRICS; FF-SHOP-REQUIREMENTS; API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING indirectly; GENERAL/RFIs on step therapy and laboratory/DMEPOS
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** CMS-0062-P; 91 Fed. Reg. 19890 (April 14, 2026)
- **Standards referenced:** Prior Authorization API; Patient Access API; Provider Access API; Payer-to-Payer API; Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR); NCPDP SCRIPT standards; CARIN Consumer Real-Time Pharmacy Benefit Check (RTPBC) IG; real-time coverage information.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Real-time patient drug cost and coverage information**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED / PATIENT-ACCESS
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Cancer patients may have multiple concurrent drugs with varying coverage rules, PA requirements, and out-of-pocket costs.
- **Specific request:** Support patient access to clear, timely, real-time drug cost and coverage information through the Patient Access API; consider CARIN RTPBC IG support.

**Topic 2: Medical-benefit drugs in the Prior Authorization API**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL
- **Position:** Support with expansion
- **Rationale:** Excluding drugs creates inconsistent requirements by drug type and payer, increasing burden and delaying cancer treatment.
- **Specific request:** Finalize inclusion of medical-benefit drugs by October 1, 2027; extend requirements to SBE/SBE-FP QHP issuers and Part D sponsors; apply the same PA standards to any drug covered by an MA plan.

**Topic 3: Pharmacy-benefit drug electronic PA standards**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Unified prescription drug PA requirements will reduce confusion and administrative burden while aligning with existing Part D standards.
- **Specific request:** Finalize NCPDP SCRIPT standards and related formulary/benefit and real-time coverage information requirements.

**Topic 4: Specific denial reasons**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DENIAL-REASONS
- **Position:** Support with modification
- **Rationale:** Generic denials prolong the time patients wait and prevent providers from quickly addressing issues.
- **Specific request:** Require clear, specific denial reasons for all drug PA denials and prohibit generic statements such as “failed to establish medical necessity” without additional detail.

**Topic 5: PA decision and notification timeframes**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS
- **Position:** Support with modification
- **Rationale:** Standardized and shorter timeframes reduce patient confusion, provider burden, and treatment delays.
- **Specific request:** Support 72-hour standard and 24-hour expedited drug PA timeframes; require MA organizations to meet a 24-hour outpatient drug PA standard in future rulemaking; shorten non-drug service timeframes to align with drug timeframes; extend standardized timeframes to QHP issuers on SBEs and SBE-FPs; require penalties and oversight for missed timeframes.

**Topic 6: Public PA metrics**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS / TRANSPARENCY
- **Position:** Support with modification
- **Rationale:** Public metrics improve transparency, but issuer-level or aggregated reporting can obscure plan variation and inappropriate PA use.
- **Specific request:** Publish metrics on CMS's website and payer websites; require plan-level reporting; report metrics by category of item or service; use the data for oversight.

**Topic 7: FF-SHOP Patient Access and Payer-to-Payer APIs**
- **Provision ID:** FF-SHOP-REQUIREMENTS
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Small group QHP members should have consistent data access and payer-to-payer continuity, especially cancer patients with complex care.
- **Specific request:** Finalize Patient Access API and Payer-to-Payer API requirements for FF-SHOP issuers; require plain-language enrollee education and opt-out explanation.

**Topic 8: Drug PA data in Access APIs and caregiver access**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED / GENERAL API updates
- **Position:** Support with clarification
- **Rationale:** Including drug PA information across APIs promotes consistency and reduces confusion.
- **Specific request:** Clarify how individuals can designate caregivers for Patient Access API information and require written communication options for enrollees who prefer them.

**Topic 9: Formulary data in Provider Access and Payer-to-Payer APIs**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED / GENERAL API updates
- **Position:** Oppose removal
- **Rationale:** Removing formulary data would force providers to search multiple sources, increasing burden and delaying care.
- **Specific request:** Reconsider proposal to remove drug formulary information from Provider Access and Payer-to-Payer APIs.

**Topic 10: Step therapy and AI oversight**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL / RFI Step Therapy
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Step therapy and AI-enabled utilization management can increase denials, burden, and delays for cancer patients whose treatments are tailored.
- **Specific request:** Require CMS staff review and human oversight of technological tools; conduct rigorous oversight and enforcement; require step therapy override processes; monitor embedded step therapy in PA requirements.

**Topic 11: Laboratory tests and DMEPOS PA**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL / RFI Laboratory Tests and DMEPOS
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Laboratory tests and DMEPOS are essential for cancer diagnosis, treatment selection, monitoring, mobility, daily functioning, and symptom management.
- **Specific request:** Hold PA for laboratory tests and DMEPOS to the same standards as other services; monitor implementation and exercise oversight when PA delays approvals.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S6 / S8 / related patient benefit IG questions:** Supports giving patients real-time drug cost and coverage information through the Patient Access API and discusses CARIN RTPBC IG value.
- **S12:** Supports incorporating medical-benefit drugs into the Prior Authorization API and says this will reduce burden and treatment delays.
- **S15:** Calls for consistent standards for all drugs and urges extension to Part D and SBE/SBE-FP QHP issuers to reduce medical/pharmacy benefit fragmentation.
- **S21:** Supports the October 1, 2027 compliance timeline for drug PA because impacted payers are already implementing non-drug requirements.
- **S28:** Urges any drug covered by an MA plan to be subject to the same PA requirements and supports Part D alignment in future rulemaking.
- **S14 / S22 / S25 / S31:** Supports NCPDP SCRIPT and pharmacy-benefit standards and formulary/real-time coverage information requirements.
- **S16:** Supports specific denial reasons and asks CMS to require more detail than generic medical-necessity language.
- **S20 / S43:** Supports 72-hour standard and 24-hour expedited drug PA timeframes and asks CMS to align non-drug timeframes with the shorter drug timeframes.
- **S29-S35:** Supports public PA metrics, numeric counts, plan-level reporting, category-level reporting, CMS publication, and oversight use.
- **S40-S42:** Supports FF-SHOP Patient Access and Payer-to-Payer API requirements, stating burden should be limited because many issuers already participate in FFEs.
- **S66-S82 / Step Therapy RFI:** Supports technology-enabled step therapy efficiency with caution; requests human oversight, override processes, and monitoring of embedded step therapy.
- **S66-S82 / Laboratory Tests and DMEPOS RFI:** Recommends applying the same PA standards to laboratory tests and DMEPOS and monitoring for delayed treatment approvals.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Finalize extension of Prior Authorization API requirements to medical-benefit drugs.
2. Extend drug PA requirements to Part D sponsors and QHP issuers on SBEs and SBE-FPs.
3. Apply the same PA standards to any drug covered by an MA plan.
4. Finalize NCPDP SCRIPT and real-time pharmacy benefit/coverage information requirements.
5. Require detailed, specific denial reasons for all drug PA denials.
6. Align PA timeframes across programs and shorten non-drug service timeframes to match drug timeframes.
7. Establish penalties and enforcement for payers that miss required PA timeframes.
8. Publish PA metrics on CMS's website and payer websites at the plan level and by service category.
9. Finalize FF-SHOP Patient Access and Payer-to-Payer API requirements.
10. Clarify caregiver access under the Patient Access API and preserve written communication options.
11. Retain formulary information in Provider Access and Payer-to-Payer APIs.
12. Require human oversight and safeguards for AI and other UM technology.
13. Require step therapy override processes and monitor embedded step therapy.
14. Apply comparable PA standards to laboratory tests and DMEPOS and monitor payer implementation.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Drug PA delays, inconsistent standards across payer/program types, generic denial reasons, inadequate non-drug PA timeframes, insufficient enforcement, aggregation of metrics, removal of formulary data, and AI/step therapy risks.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Treatment delays, disease progression, provider administrative burden, patient confusion, delayed appeals, worse outcomes for cancer patients, and additional patient costs.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Fragmented payer scope, lack of plan-level data, lack of category-level metrics, absence of penalties, caregiver access ambiguity, and technology/AI oversight needs.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** ACS CAN's 2024 report found Part D plans required PA for CDK 4/6 inhibitors 97% of the time; embedded step therapy occurred in 23% of cases for Ibrance, 22% for Kisqali and Kisqali Femara co-pack, and 88% for Verzenio.
- **Studies or research referenced:** AMA article on AI and prior authorization denials; ACS CAN 2024 Step Therapy in Medicare Part D Oncology Drugs report.
- **Examples provided:** Cancer patients with multiple concurrent prescriptions; outpatient and physician-administered therapies; CDK 4/6 inhibitors; laboratory testing for cancer diagnosis and monitoring; DMEPOS for mobility and symptom management.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Cancer patients, caregivers, providers, MA organizations, Medicaid/CHIP programs, QHP issuers, Part D sponsors, FF-SHOP issuers, and payers using utilization management tools.

- **Technical feasibility:** Supports the October 2027 timeline and API expansion; requests clarification and safeguards around caregiver access, written communication, formulary data, and technology oversight.
- **Patient care impact:** Very high. The comment repeatedly ties timely drug access, PA decisions, lab testing, and DMEPOS access to cancer outcomes and disease progression.
